report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

info.title: Pooled Multiplex Amplicon Massive Parallel Sequencing for High-Throughput Confirmation of Whole-Genome Sequencing Potentially Pathogenic Variants in Patients with Parkinsonism

text.text: Whole-genome sequencing identifies large numbers of genetic variants, although only a subset requires independent confirmation for clinical interpretation.
Sanger sequencing remains the standard confirmation method but is impractical for large-scale variant verification.
We developed and evaluated a strategy for variant confirmation based on multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing of pooled DNA samples.
Whole-genome sequencing data were obtained from 86 individuals, including patients with parkinsonism and controls.
Variants were selected using phenotype-driven filtering, ClinVar classification, and pathogenicity assessment criteria.
A total of 307 variants were targeted using a custom amplicon panel comprising 290 amplicons.
DNA samples were normalized, pooled into 16 mixtures, and sequenced following automated library preparation.
Variant presence and sequencing quality were assessed using standard bioinformatic tools.
Of the 307 selected variants, 243 were successfully confirmed.

Unconfirmed variants included sequencing artifacts (18), insufficiently covered targets (5), large insertions or deletions exceeding 12 base pairs (36), and variants located within homopolymeric regions (5).
Results for selected variants were concordant with Sanger sequencing, and observed variant frequencies corresponded to expected frequencies in pooled samples.
This approach provides a robust, rapid, and cost-effective method for highthroughput genetic variants confirming identified by whole-genome sequencing while requiring only limited DNA input.
Despite complete concordance with Sanger sequencing, larger validation studies are needed before multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing can replace routine confirmatory testing.
• Design and application of a high-throughput verification strategy for WGS variants with minimal DNA input requirements • Reliable and independent confirmation of WGS findings .
• Detection of point mutations, small indels and duplications.

High-throughput molecular genetic sequencing analyses can be broadly categorized based on the extent of human genome coverage into targeted sequencing, whole exome sequencing (WES), and whole genome sequencing (WGS).
Targeted sequencing focuses on specific genes or genomic regions-ranging from several to hundreds of genes-that are known to be associated with a particular disease.

This approach typically yields hundreds to thousands of genetic variants per sample, among which only a limited number are clinically relevant. [1] [2] [3] Whole exome sequencing expands the scope to all protein-coding regions of the genome, encompassing approximately 1-2% of the genome but capturing the majority of known disease-causing variants. [4] [5] [6] WES can identify up to hundreds of thousands of variants per individual, with dozens potentially having clinical significance.

text.text: The most comprehensive approach is WGS, which covers the entire genomic DNA sequence, including coding and non-coding regions, regulatory elements, and structural variants. 3, 7, 8 This approach provides a comprehensive amount of genetic information, detecting approximately 3-5 million single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions/deletions (indels), as well as thousands of larger structural variants per individual. 9, 10 In our study, WGS was performed on 86 unique DNA samples collected from an isolated population in the Hornacko region (South Eastern Moravia, Czech Republic), a population characterized by a high and familial burden of Parkinsonism. 11 Such isolated populations represent invaluable resources in genetic research due to reduced genetic heterogeneity and increased prevalence of founder mutations. 12, 13 Each sample generated approximately 5 million SNVs and indels, along with thousands of structural variants, dozens of which may have potential clinical impact.

text.text: Applying Sanger sequencing to verify the vast number of variants from WGS across all 86 samples would be highly laborious, costly, and would consume considerable amounts of DNA and reagents.

Large-scale studies show that Sanger sequencing confirms over 99.9% of NGS variants, however, routine Sanger confirmation adds cost and time with limited benefit, and best practices now suggest restricting confirmation to select cases. text.text: The aims of this study: 1) To design and apply a strategy for the verification of WGS variants that is not demanding on the initial amount of DNA and can, within the same sequencing run, reliably, independently and within the available time verify WGS findings.
This strategy is based on multi-amplicon massively parallel sequencing of mixed samples.

The amplicon sequencing strategy should be predominantly focused on the detection of point mutations, small deletions and insertions (indels) up to 12 bp 2) To use the Sanger sequencing approach for NGS result validation and for resolving ambiguous results (low coverage, homopolymeric or repetitive regions or insertion/deletion larger than 12 bp) 3) For confirmed variants, the expected allele ratios were compared with the observed ratios obtained from the sequencing data.
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Palacky University and University Hospital Olomouc, Czechia.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants after they were thoroughly informed about the study.

The patient cohort included: 21 patients from the Hornacko region 44 controls from the Hornacko region 21 polysymptomatic patients outside the Hornacko region This study does not address the clinical impact of the identified variants.
Therefore, given the objectives of the study, detailed demographic and clinical characteristics of the entire cohort are not provided by the authors.

text.text: Peripheral blood (9 ml), collected in EDTA tubes, served as the primary biological material for DNA isolation.
DNA was isolated from 74 whole blood samples using the salting-out method 27 , and from 12 whole blood samples using the magnetic bead-based extraction (MagNA Pure, Roche Diagnostics).

text.text: Samples obtained using both extraction procedures were subsequently normalized to the same DNA concentration of 10 ng/µL and pooled irrespective of the extraction method.

Selection of variants from WGS data: Whole genome sequencing analyses were performed using the Illumina TruSeq DNA PCR-free library preparation kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) and sequenced on the NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA).
Data analysis and variant annotation were conducted using Varsome Clinical 13.1.6 (Saphetor SA, Lausanne, Switzerland).
In each analyzed sample, approximately 5 million variants were identified, with about 200,000 located in exonic and splicing regions.
The selection of variants for the confirmation was based on two primary filtering strategies using Varsome Clinical.

The first filter focused on genes and variants associated with Parkinsonism, including the following phenotypes: Parkinsonism (HP:0001300), Parkinsonism with favorable response to dopaminergic medication (HP:0002548), and Juvenile-onset Parkinson's disease (MONDO:0000828).

This filter included 178 genes (Supplemental Table S1) selected according to VarSome Clinical version 13.1.2. 28 Variants were further filtered using a population allele frequency threshold of <0.001 (gnomAD v3.1.2) and ACMG criteria with the classification as pathogenic, likely pathogenic and variant of uncertain significance (VUS).

text.text: The second filter was based on ClinVar classification, selecting only variants annotated as pathogenic or likely pathogenic (to the date 11.10.2025).
After applying both filters, a total of 307 variants (including 14 from mitochondrial (mt) DNA) were selected for confirmation (138 SNVs, 126 small indels and 43 larger indels ≥ 12).
The primers for independent confirmation were successfully designed using Ion AmpliSeq™ Custom Panels via the AmpliSeq Designer tool (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).
In total, 290 unique amplicons were used to evaluate the selected 307 variants.

text.text: DNA mixture preparation:
Eighty-six DNA samples were first normalized to a uniform concentration of 10 ng/µL using Qubit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and then pooled into 16 DNA mixtures.
The first 10 mixtures each contained DNA from 5 individual samples, while the remaining 6 mixtures included DNA from 6 samples each.
Each pooled mixture was further diluted in nuclease-free water to a final concentration of 0.7 ng/µL.

Automated library preparation was performed in a single run using the Ion Chef™ Instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and the AmpliSeq™ Kit for Chef DL8 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), following the manufacturer's protocol (Ion AmpliSeq Library Preparation on the Ion Chef System, MAN0013432, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).

text.text: A total of 307 unique WGS-derived variants were included in the maMPS panel.
Because several variants were present in more than one individual, this corresponded to 693 individual variant observations across the 86 samples.
Overall, 243 of 307 unique variants were confirmed by maMPS.

Of these, 189 variants fulfilled the standard A1 confirmation criteria, 24 fulfilled the A2 criteria, one variant fulfilled A1 or A2 depending on the individual mixture, and 29 variants were classified according to the A3 criteria for homopolymeric regions.
Among the remaining 64 unique variants, 18 were not detected by maMPS despite technically evaluable sequencing conditions and were classified as maMPS-unconfirmed/presumed WGS artifacts (Rule B).

Five variants could not be assessed because of insufficient coverage (C1), five were non-evaluable because of homopolymeric sequence context (C2), and 36 represented indels ≥12 bp that could not be reliably assessed using the current amplicon design (C3).
After excluding large indels ≥12 bp, 254 of 264 SNVs and small indels (96.2%) were technically evaluable using the proposed workflow.

NGS has become a common standard in clinical genetics testing.
In clinical practice, NGS workflows are often optimized for high sensitivity, which may lead to an increased rate of false-positive results.
Nevertheless, high accuracy and reliability in the detection of genetic variants are essential for clinical diagnosis.

Multiple professional organizations now recommend that each laboratory develop its own policy for orthogonal confirmation, considering factors such as test content, sequencing platform, variant type, and quality metrics.

Universal confirmation is no longer required; instead, confirmation should be targeted to variants with lower sequencing quality confidence or unexpected results. 19, 25 Laboratories are encouraged to document and regularly review their confirmation policies. 19, 25 Traditionally, Sanger sequencing has been considered the gold standard for orthogonal confirmation of NGS-detected variants, helping to reduce the risk of false positives (FPs).

text.text: The novelty of the present approach does not lie in amplicon-based sequencing itself, which is an established methodology, but in the design of the confirmation workflow.
Individual DNA samples were combined into predefined mixtures, thereby reducing 86 individual samples to 16 sequencing libraries.
Because the composition of each pool was known, an expected allele fraction could be calculated for each selected WGS variant.

Confirmation therefore relied on three complementary features: detection using an independent sequencing platform, occurrence in the expected DNA mixture, and agreement with the theoretically expected allele ratio.
This combination provides an additional verification layer while considerably reducing the number of individual sequencing libraries required.

Considering the limited amount of available and often unique DNA, the study design was optimized to allow the assessment of hundreds of variants presented in mixed samples in a heterozygous state with an expected allele ratio as low as 1/12, provided sufficient sequencing coverage was achieved.
The study confirmed the well-known limitation of evaluating variants in homopolymeric or repetitive regions.
These regions were evaluated using a correction for false-positive variant calls (see Methods -Variant evaluation).
Overall, five variants located within homopolymeric regions could not be reliably assessed (rs1203776328, rs35978415, rs952840023, rs113262693 and rs902007551).
Another limiting aspect was the evaluation of indels larger than 12 bp.

As we anticipated a higher degree of DNA fragmentation in a substantial proportion of samples stored in the DNA biobank for more than 10 years, we used a pipeline optimized for the verification of SNPs and small indels during amplicon custom design.
Consequently, indels larger than 12 bp were frequently not detectable (36 out of 43 variants).

Exceptions included seven variants (rs1278020632, rs553779459, rs111033253, rs1790142871, rs879074973, NM_020919.4:c.2417+2308_2417+2309insTCCAAAATATAG p.?, ENST00000394991.8:c.306+38698_306+38699insTATCCAGAAAGTTATTT, p.?,).
To improve the detection of larger indels, a more appropriate strategy would be to use amplicons of the largest possible size.
In the case of the AmpliSeq Designer, amplicons of up to 375 bp could be considered.
Alternatively, additional verification using conventional Sanger sequencing or long-read technology may be used.
All 14 mtDNA variants were reliably confirmed in all samples, including two with 12% and 13% heteroplasmy, as determined by WGS.
An important limitation of the present study is the relatively small number of variants subjected to independent Sanger sequencing.

Although all maMPS-confirmed variants included in this subset were concordant with Sanger sequencing, the analysis of 19 variants does not provide sufficient evidence to conclude that maMPS can universally replace Sanger-based confirmation.
Rather, the present results support its use as a scalable complementary confirmation strategy that may substantially reduce the number of individual Sanger analyses required.

A larger systematic comparison with orthogonal sequencing would be necessary to establish analytical sensitivity and specificity and to define circumstances in which Sanger confirmation could be safely omitted.
This question will be addressed in our forthcoming follow-up validation study, which will build directly upon the findings of the present work.

In our expected versus observed analysis, p0 corresponds to a theoretical DNA mixing ratio and does not reflect biological variation.
Therefore, a significant binomial test reflects a deviation from expected laboratory ratio and may be caused by several non-biological factors.
Four major mechanisms are listed below.
a) Pipetting and quantification variability.
DNA mixtures depend on accurate volumes and reliable concentration measurements.
Pipetting introduces imprecision, and quantification adds additional error, especially at low DNA inputs. 47, 48 These inaccuracies may alter sample proportions. b) Uneven coverage and locus dropout.

After excluding the indel ≥12 bp variants that were deemed unreliable or non-evaluable by this method, we were able to accurately and reliably assess 254 out of 264 (over 96 %) of the SNPs and small indels.

Our approach demonstrates robust performance, and with the incorporation of longer reads it could also be extended to verify larger genomic alterations, thereby increasing its applicability in genetic research and diagnostics of Parkinsonism and similar polygenic disorders.

Although maMPS showed complete concordance with Sanger sequencing in the tested subset, larger validation studies are required before it can be considered a replacement for routine Sanger-based confirmation.
